quote_item6: the 2020 study supplemented this base by adding 1,240 domains from NewsGuard that were rated as "repeatedly publishing false content," resulting in a total of 1,796 general untrustworthy domains. For the 2024 study, we updated the NewsGuard data to include an additional 777 domains rated since 2020, yielding a final list of 2,573 general untrustworthy domains.
quote_item10: In 2024, 16.5% (95% CI [13.7%, 19.4%]) of Americans visited at least one untrustworthy website, a significant decline from the 26.1% (95% CI [22.5%, 29.8%]) who did so in 2020
notes: Dahlke, Moore & Hancock, preregistered, 2024 US election. YouGov Pulse web-tracking panel of 1,069 US adults paired with a two-wave survey, 8 October - 12 November 2024, ~6M visits; contributes 15 estimates, all REACH shares of panellists (overall, AI-generated subset, and age/party/ideology subgroups). Item1 LOW: US adults, with YouGov demographic weights applied to every reported estimate. Item2 LOW: a national online panel plus on-device passive logging is a fair route to that population. Item3 LOW: the exposure measure is a complete URL-level behavioural trace of every visit, not a sample of browsing. Item4 UNCLEAR (treated as HIGH): participants had to consent to install Pulse software on their devices, and no invitation, response or attrition figure appears anywhere; the weights are demographic (age, gender, race/ethnicity) and do not touch willingness to be tracked, which the limitations section never raises. Item5 LOW: trace from the subjects' own devices. Item6 LOW: the list is Grinberg et al. plus Allcott & Gentzkow plus NewsGuard 'repeatedly publishing false content' ratings, and the AI subset is NewsGuard's UAINS database with its four published criteria - the exact class of published third-party credibility list the 2026-07-23 ruling covers. Item7 LOW: the component lists are published, externally maintained instruments, rated consistently with every other Grinberg/NewsGuard study in this corpus; no per-domain accuracy statistic is reported and the authors concede domain-level coding cannot capture within-domain variance. Item8 LOW: one Pulse pipeline covering desktop and mobile for everyone in the 2024 wave. Item9 LOW: the window is stated exactly, four weeks before and one week after election day. Item10 LOW: numerator is panellists with at least one visit to a listed domain, denominator is all 1,069 tracked panellists and their whole browsing stream; the subgroup denominators (65+, 18-29, Republicans, Democrats, Trump and Harris supporters, ideology bands) are real subpopulations, not selected-on-outcome subsets. Recorded as source-level REACH: this is the share who visited a flagged SITE, not the share who met a false claim. Two carried figures come from earlier waves measured with earlier list versions (2.6% AI-generated in 2020; the authors state the 2020 statistics used the 2020 list and the 2024 statistics the updated list), so the over-time comparison is not instrument-constant - noted rather than charged, since it does not affect the 2024 denominators.

quote_item6: we investigated the prevalence of low-quality or 'fake news' URLs using sources listed by Media Bias Fact Check (Weld, Glenski, and Althoff 2021)
quote_item10: finding them to constitute less than 0.01% of the total urls shared
notes: Couto & Garimella, arXiv 2024. Facebook data donation: 1,261 US users recruited through the PureSpectrum survey panel donated the public pages and groups they follow (251,220 entities), a random 10% of which were loaded into CrowdTangle, yielding 32.0M posts published October 2022 - September 2023, 16.6M of them English. Item1 LOW: the target population is US Facebook users, a real public, not a universe defined by the outcome. Item2 LOW: a commercial survey panel is a recognised route to that population, and the authors reweight with Facebook's balance library on age, gender and ethnicity. Item3 HIGH: the authors themselves call it 'the convenient nature of our sampling', with women oversampled and 18-24s undersampled; propensity reweighting corrects the demographic margins, not the selection mechanism. Item4 UNCLEAR (treated as HIGH): no invited denominator, no donation or completion rate, and nothing on how donors differ from non-donors beyond the three weighting variables - handing over a Facebook account is a more selective act than answering a survey. Item5 HIGH: this is the decisive item. Exposure is never observed. What is measured is every URL POSTED by the pages and groups a user follows, pulled from CrowdTangle - publisher-side supply inferred as audience consumption, which is the anchor's named example. Item6 LOW: Media Bias/Fact Check is named explicitly in the source-level ruling as an acceptable external case definition. Item7 LOW: MBFC via Weld, Glenski and Althoff (2021) is a published, externally maintained list, rated as such throughout this corpus - though no list size, vintage or URL-matching procedure is given here. Item8 LOW: one donation tool, one CrowdTangle pipeline, one period, English-only for everyone. Item9 LOW: a stated twelve-month window, October 2022 to September 2023. Item10 HIGH: the denominator is 'the total urls shared' by followed pages and groups - a supply-side corpus, further reduced by the random 10% entity subsample, the English-only filter, and the fact that link posts are only 27% of content - not any audience's whole diet; no numerator count is printed at all, only the ceiling 'less than 0.01%'. The entire misinformation result is one sentence in a paper about political-content consumption, with no methods paragraph behind it.

quote_item6: We leverage GPT-4o to classify images as AI-generated or non-AI-generated.
quote_item10: Overall, approximately 12.33% of images related to the 2024 U.S. Election on X are AI-generated according to GPT-4o classification.
notes: Chen, Ye, Tsai, Ferrara & Luceri, HT 2025. Content analysis of an existing keyword-queried X/Twitter corpus on the 2024 US election, 1 July - 30 September 2024: 2.5M images shared by 414K spreaders, classified by GPT-4o. Contributes two appendix-pool estimates: 12% of shared images detected AI-generated, and 10% of image spreaders accounting for 80% of AI-generated image shares. Item1 HIGH: the universe is a curated topical corpus built by 'querying targeted keywords related to political figures, events, and emerging issues', not any audience or public. Item2 HIGH: that keyword-seeded frame supports the general claim 'what proportion of all images on X are AI-generated?'. Item3 LOW: within the frame every image was submitted to the detector (2,462,132 processed) - a census, not top-N selection; 9.5% returned invalid responses, many of them content-moderation refusals, which is plausibly non-random missingness on exactly the sensitive images of interest. Items4-5 NA (content-only design; users are observed only through the keyword-filtered corpus, not through any complete behavioural trace). Item6 HIGH: nothing in this paper is defined as false. The label is AI PROVENANCE applied by the authors' own GPT-4o pipeline - a truthful AI-illustrated image carries it - so a non-falsity attribute stands in for falsity, with no external ground truth for misinformation anywhere in the text. Item7 LOW: the best-validated instrument in this batch - F1 0.96 on a 2,400-image validation set, 0.92 and 0.94 under rotation and rescaling, and an in-the-wild audit of 2,000 sampled images by two independent annotators with Cohen's kappa 0.87, FPR 6.5%, FNR 1.6%. Item8 LOW: one platform, one corpus, one detector, one window. Item9 LOW: a stated three-month window. Item10 HIGH: the denominator is election-keyword images on X, not any audience's diet, and the question it is offered as answering ('what proportion of all images on X') is far wider than the denominator supports; the 12.33% is also computed on the 90.5% of images returning valid responses, which the sentence does not say. INSTRUMENT MISFIT, flagged not overridden: item 6 is HIGH because the anchor asks for an external falsity standard and there is none, but the paper never claims to measure falsity and the freeze already quarantines both estimates to the appendix ai_provenance pool for that reason. Items 6 and 10 both HIGH sets overall HIGH at n_high = 4 under the pre-specified weighting.

quote_item6: Our list combines the 223 channels classified by Ledwich and Zaitsev (26) as Men's Rights Activists or Anti-Social Justice Warriors, the 141 Intellectual Dark Web and Alt-lite channels from Ribeiro et al. (24), and the 24 channels from Lewis' Alternative Influence Network (35).
quote_item10: As Fig. 2 indicates, 1.7% (95% CI, 0.0 to 5.6) of participants account for 80% of total time spent on videos from alternative channels.
notes: Chen, Nyhan, Reifler, Robertson & Wilson, Science Advances 2023. Browser-extension panel of 1,181 US participants drawn from 4,000 YouGov respondents, 21 July - 31 December 2020, median 133 days enrolled; contributes the two appendix-pool concentration figures (1.7% of participants for 80% of alternative-channel watch time, 0.6% for extremist channels). Item1 LOW: the target population is US adults - the base is a nationally representative 2018 CCES sample and the two oversamples (high resentment, heavy YouTube use) are a design feature undone by YouGov weights applied to every reported estimate, not a population defined by the outcome. Item2 LOW: the YouGov panel is a fair route to that population. Item3 LOW: the exposure measure is a complete behavioural trace of browsing plus HTML snapshots, not a sample of content. Item4 LOW: the participation chain is reported in full - 1,181 of 4,000 installed the extension, broken out as 778, 97 and 306 by subsample - weights are applied throughout, and the authors state plainly that the sample 'is of course not fully representative of the U.S. adult population'; the 9.7% install rate in the high-resentment oversample runs AGAINST the quantity estimated (it thins the heavy consumers), and the weights address it. Item5 LOW: trace from the subjects' own browsers. Item6 LOW under the source-level ruling: the alternative and extremist channel lists are unions of published third-party rosters (Ledwich & Zaitsev, Ribeiro et al., Lewis, the ADL Center on Extremism, and Sankin's compilation from the SPLC, the Canadian Anti-Hate Network and the Counter Extremism Project) - external and pre-existing, which is the line the ruling draws. Item7 LOW: the constituent lists are published expert instruments, the union is documented with overlap counts (36.2% of extremist channels on two or more source lists), the mainstream comparison list is screened on NewsGuard 60+ and the Grinberg black/red lists, and the browser data are validated against browser history in the SI; the compiled lists are deliberately not released, which makes the classification unauditable but leaves the instruments themselves published. Item8 LOW: one extension, Chrome/Firefox, one window; mobile and in-app viewing is uncaptured, a coverage limit applied uniformly rather than a mixed mode. Item9 LOW: the window is stated exactly. Item10 LOW: the numerator is participants and the denominator is total observed watch time on alternative (or extremist) channel videos across the whole weighted panel of 1,181 - a defined total over a real audience, which is what the item asks; the CIs are very wide (0.0 to 5.6 and 0.0 to 4.6) because only 15.4% viewed any alternative video and 6.1% any extremist video, but precision is a descriptor, not a Hoy bias item. INSTRUMENT MISFIT, flagged not overridden: 'alternative' and 'extremist' are ideology-and-harm labels, not veracity labels - the paper's own words are 'we define both alternative and extremist channels as potentially harmful' - so a truthful video from a listed channel counts. My own judgement is that this is not a misinformation case definition at all, but the ruling's stated test for item 6 is external and pre-existing versus internal and ad hoc, not which external standard is best, and these lists are external and pre-existing; the freeze already handles the construct gap by putting both estimates in the appendix harm_category pool. Rating LOW per the anchor, with the disagreement recorded here.
